title: Functional Frontier: Families and Naming
welcome_lead: Survey the families of organic molecules and IUPAC naming.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on functional groups and nomenclature.
final_note: You can name the molecules of life and industry.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Identify longest carbon chain containing the functional group; this gives the suffix.

Number atoms so functional group has lowest locant. Name substituents alphabetically with locants.

Priority: COOH > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene > alkyne > halide.

Highest priority group becomes suffix, others become prefixes (e.g. hydroxy- for -OH if outranked).

Structural: chain, position, functional group. Stereoisomerism: E/Z (cis/trans), optical (chiral, R/S).

E/Z requires C=C with two different groups on each end. Optical requires 4 different groups on a carbon (chiral centre).

mcqs.q: What is the product of mild oxidation of a primary alcohol?
options: A primary alcohol is oxidised directly to a ketone.
An aldehyde (which can be further oxidised to a carboxylic acid).
A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.

mcqs.q: How do alkenes typically react with bromine?
options: The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
Stereoisomers have different numbers of atoms but the same molecular formula.
By electrophilic addition — bromine adds across the double bond to form a dibromoalkane.
Bromine substitutes for a hydrogen on the alkene, releasing HBr.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes structural isomers from stereoisomers?
options: Structural isomers have different atom connectivity; stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement.
A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
Stereoisomers are just structural isomers drawn from a different angle.
Stereoisomers have different numbers of atoms but the same molecular formula.
